title: Europeans treat culture as community infrastructure and democratic expression while questioning artist livelihoods and AI’s creative-economic effects
source_unit: European Commission, Special Eurobarometer on Europeans' attitudes towards culture, fielded February-April 2025 and published 8 May 2025
geography: European Union citizens across all 27 Member States

denominator.unit: more than EU citizens responding to the Special Eurobarometer survey across 27 Member States

culture_exchange_belonging.unit: percent agreeing culture and cultural exchange should have a very important place in the EU so citizens from different countries can feel more European

heritage_importance.unit: percent saying cultural heritage is important for Europe

local_welfare.unit: percent saying culture and the arts are important for the welfare and economic development of the place where they live

community_route.value: culture, shared values, and history are treated as central sources of community feeling and European belonging

observations.method: European Commission Special Eurobarometer survey conducted February-April 2025 across the 27 EU Member States.
observations.uncertainty: The findings measure attitudes and perceived importance rather than actual cultural access, participation equality, local investment, or the causal effect of culture on belonging.
observations.subgroup: EU citizens, local communities, cultural participants, heritage communities, artists, cultural organizations, and EU and national policymakers.
observations.counterinterpretation: High stated cultural importance can coexist with unequal access, declining local provision, or disagreement over which identities and histories receive recognition.

denominator.unit: more than EU citizens responding to the Special Eurobarometer across 27 Member States

artistic_expression_importance.unit: percent saying freedom of artistic expression is important to them

perceived_freedom.unit: percent agreeing artists can freely express ideas and opinions without fear of government censorship or retaliation

country_variation.value: perceptions of artistic freedom vary between EU countries

democratic_route.value: artistic freedom is framed as part of a healthy democracy and a cultural-rights infrastructure rather than only a sector concern

observations.method: EU-wide public-opinion survey with Member State comparisons on cultural values and artistic expression.
observations.uncertainty: Perceived freedom is not a legal or incident-based measure of censorship, retaliation, self-censorship, or working conditions; cross-country variation needs contextual interpretation.
observations.subgroup: Artists, cultural workers, audiences, minority and regional cultural communities, governments, funders, and democratic institutions.
observations.counterinterpretation: High support for artistic freedom does not ensure support for controversial works or protect artists from non-state economic, platform, or social pressure.

observations.period: 2025; generative AI, artist work, and cultural value

denominator.unit: more than EU citizens responding to the Special Eurobarometer across 27 Member States

ai_art_recognition.unit: percent saying they can tell the difference between an AI-created piece of art and one crafted by a human

ai_artist_concern.unit: percent concerned generative AI may affect artists' employment or earnings

artist_fair_pay.unit: percent believing artists in their country generally receive fair and appropriate remuneration

labor_route.value: public concern about AI’s creative and employment effects is occurring alongside a weak sense that artists are fairly paid

observations.method: EU-wide survey of public attitudes toward generative AI, artistic labor, and cultural-sector conditions.
observations.uncertainty: Concern and recognition measures are perceptions, not forecasts of AI labor displacement, quality judgments, or artist income; fair-pay assessments may reflect limited knowledge of cultural work.
observations.subgroup: Artists, cultural workers, audiences, creators using AI, cultural employers, platforms, rights holders, and policymakers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Generative AI may create new creative tools or markets while also redistributing value; public concern does not specify which governance or compensation mechanism would work.

denominator.unit: more than EU citizens responding to the 2025 Special Eurobarometer, with comparison to the 2013 cultural participation survey

recent_participation.unit: percent reporting participation in artistic activities such as dancing, singing, or playing an instrument during the prior 12 months

change_since_2013.value: the 2025 participation share is about one third higher than the 37 percent reported in 2013

policy_priorities.value: respondents prioritize making arts more accessible, protecting heritage, fair pay and conditions for cultural workers, artistic freedom, and skills development

participation_route.value: cultural participation is treated as both a lived activity and a policy lever for inclusion, cohesion, democratic values, and creative-sector sustainability

observations.method: Special Eurobarometer cultural-participation question with comparison to the 2013 Eurobarometer measure; policy priorities drawn from the same survey.
observations.uncertainty: Question wording, recall, social desirability, and sample or survey changes can affect comparisons across 2013 and 2025; participation frequency, affordability, and subgroup equality are not fully captured by the headline share.
observations.subgroup: EU residents, amateur and professional artists, cultural audiences, heritage users, cultural institutions, and creative-sector workers.
observations.counterinterpretation: A higher aggregate participation share may conceal concentration among advantaged groups or participation in low-cost informal activities rather than broad access to cultural institutions.

related_sources.claim: The Eurobarometer survey detail page provides the full report and Member State fact sheets for Europeans' attitudes towards culture.
The European Commission's Culture and Democracy evidence review provides research context on cultural participation and civic engagement.

boundary: This record adds EU-wide public-opinion evidence on culture as community and democratic infrastructure, artistic freedom, generative AI concerns, artist remuneration, and cultural participation. It is aggregate survey evidence, not respondent-level ingestion, a causal culture-and-democracy estimate, a cultural labor-market panel, or proof that stated importance translates into equal access.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official European Commission culture page reviewed for survey size and field period, community and welfare importance, artistic freedom, generative-AI and artist-pay concerns, participation change, and policy priorities.
